speaker: MODERATOR
text: Good evening from the Clark Athletic Center at the University of Massachusetts in Boston.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: I’m Jim Lehrer of the NewsHour on PBS, and I welcome you to the first of three 90-minute debates between the Democratic candidate for president, Vice President Al Gore and the Republican candidate, Governor George W.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Bush of Texas.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: The debates are sponsored by the Commission on Presidential Debates and they will be conducted within formats and rules agreed to between the commission and the two campaigns.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: We’ll have the candidates at podiums.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: No answer to a question can exceed two minutes.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Rebuttal is limited to one minute.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: But as moderator I have the option to follow up and to extend any particular give and take another three-and-a-half minutes.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Even then, no single answer can exceed two minutes.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: The candidates under their rules may not question each other directly.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: There will be no opening statements, but each candidate may have up to two minutes for a closing statement.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: The questions and the subjects were chosen by me alone.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: I have told no one from the two campaigns, or the Commission, or anyone else involved what they are.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: There is a small audience in the hall tonight.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: They are not here to participate, only to listen.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: I have asked, and they have agreed, to remain silent for the next 90 minutes.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Except for right now, when they will applaud as we welcome the two candidates, Governor Bush and Vice President Gore.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: And now the first question as determined by a flip of a coin, it goes to Vice President Gore.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Vice President Gore, you have questioned whether Governor Bush has the experience to be President of the United States.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: What exactly do you mean?

speaker: GORE
text: Well, Jim, first of all, I would like to thank the sponsors of this debate and the people of Boston for hosting the debate.

speaker: GORE
text: I would like to thank Governor Bush for participating, and I would like to say I’m happy to be here with Tipper and our family.

speaker: GORE
text: I have actually not questioned Governor Bush’s experience.

speaker: GORE
text: I have questioned his proposals.

speaker: GORE
text: And here is why.

speaker: GORE
text: I think this is a very important moment for our country.

speaker: GORE
text: We have achieved extraordinary prosperity.

speaker: GORE
text: And in this election, America has to make an important choice.

speaker: GORE
text: Will we use our prosperity to enrich not just the few, but all of our families?

speaker: GORE
text: I believe we have to make the right and responsible choices.

speaker: GORE
text: If I’m entrusted with the presidency, here are the choices that I will make.

speaker: GORE
text: I will balance the budget every year.

speaker: GORE
text: I will pay down the national debt.

speaker: GORE
text: I will put Medicare and Social Security in a lockbox and protect them.

speaker: GORE
text: And I will cut taxes for middle-class families.

speaker: GORE
text: I believe it’s important to resist the temptation to squander our surplus.

speaker: GORE
text: If we make the right choices, we can have a prosperity that endures and enriches all of our people.

speaker: GORE
text: If I’m entrusted with the presidency, I will help parents and strengthen families because, you know, if we have prosperity that grows and grows, we still won’t be successful unless we strengthen families by, for example, ensuring that children can always go to schools that are safe.

speaker: GORE
text: By giving parents the tools to protect their children against cultural pollution.

speaker: GORE
text: I will make sure that we invest in our country and our families.

speaker: GORE
text: And I mean investing in education, health care, the environment, and middle-class tax cuts and retirement security.

speaker: GORE
text: That is my agenda and that is why I think that it’s not just a question of experience.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Governor Bush, one minute rebuttal.

speaker: BUSH
text: Well, we do come from different places.

speaker: BUSH
text: I come from West Texas.

speaker: BUSH
text: The governor is the chief executive officer.

speaker: BUSH
text: We know how to set agendas.

speaker: BUSH
text: I think you’ll find the difference reflected in our budgets.

speaker: BUSH
text: I want to take one-half of the surplus and dedicate it to Social Security.

speaker: BUSH
text: One-quarter of the surplus for important projects, and I want to send one-quarter of the surplus back to the people who pay the bills.

speaker: BUSH
text: I want everybody who pays taxes to have their tax rates cut.

speaker: BUSH
text: And that stands in contrast to my worthy opponent’s plan, which will increase the size of government dramatically.

speaker: BUSH
text: His plan is three times larger than President Clinton’s proposed plan eight years ago.

speaker: BUSH
text: It is a plan that will have 200 new programs — expanded programs and creates 20,000 new bureaucrats.

speaker: BUSH
text: It it empowers Washington.

speaker: BUSH
text: Tonight youâ€™re going to hear that my passion and my vision is to empower Americans to be able to make decisions for themselves in their own lives.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: So I take it by your answer, then, Mr.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Vice President, that in an interview recently with the “New York Times” when you said that you questioned whether or not Governor Bush has experience enough to be president, you were talking about strictly policy differences.

speaker: GORE
text: Yes, Jim.

speaker: GORE
text: I said that his tax cut plan, for example, raises the question of whether it’s the right choice for the country.

speaker: GORE
text: And let me give you an example of what I mean.

speaker: GORE
text: Under Governor Bush’s tax cut proposal, he would spend more money on tax cuts for the wealthiest 1% than all of the new spending that he proposes for education, health care, prescription drugs and national defense all combined.

speaker: GORE
text: Now, I think those are the wrong priorities.

speaker: GORE
text: Now, under my proposal, for every dollar that I propose in spending for things like education and health care, I will put another dollar into middle class tax cuts.

speaker: GORE
text: And for every dollar that I spend in those two categories, I’ll put $2 toward paying down the national debt.

speaker: GORE
text: I think it’s very important to keep the debt going down and completely eliminate it.

speaker: GORE
text: And I also think it’s very important to go to the next stage of welfare reform.

speaker: GORE
text: Our country has cut the welfare rolls in half.

speaker: GORE
text: I fought hard from my days in the Senate and as vice president to cut the welfare rolls and we’ve moved millions of people in America into good jobs.

speaker: GORE
text: But it’s now time for the next stage of welfare reform, and include fathers and not only mothers.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: We’re going to get a lot of those.

speaker: BUSH
text: Let me just say that obviously tonight we’re going to hear some phony numbers about what I think and what we ought to do.

speaker: BUSH
text: People need to know that over the next ten years it is going to be $25 trillion of revenue that comes into our treasurey and we anticipate spending $21 trillion.

speaker: BUSH
text: And my plan say why don’t we pass 1.

speaker: BUSH
text: 3 trillion of that back to the people who pay the bills?

speaker: BUSH
text: Surely we can afford 5% of the $25 trillion that are coming into the treasury to the hard working people that pay the bills.

speaker: BUSH
text: There is a difference of opinion.

speaker: BUSH
text: My opponent thinks the government — the surplus is the government’s money.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s not what I think.

speaker: BUSH
text: I think it’s the hard-working people of America’s money and I want to share some of that money with you so you have more money to build and save and dream for your families.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s a difference of opinion.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s a difference between government making decisions for you and you getting more of your money to make decisions for yourself.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Let me just follow up one quick question.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: When you hear Vice President Gore question your experience, do you read it the same way, that he’s talking about policy differences only?

speaker: BUSH
text: Yes.

speaker: BUSH
text: I take him for his word.

speaker: BUSH
text: Look, I fully recognize I’m not of Washington.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’m from Texas.

speaker: BUSH
text: And he’s got a lot of experience, but so do I.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I’ve been the chief executive officer of the second biggest state in the union.

speaker: BUSH
text: I have a proud record of working with both Republicans and Democrats, which is what our nation needs.

speaker: BUSH
text: Somebody that can come to Washington and say let’s forget all the finger pointing and get positive things done on Medicare, prescription drugs, Social Security, and so I take him for his word.

speaker: GORE
text: Jim, if I could just respond.

speaker: GORE
text: I know that.

speaker: GORE
text: The governor used the phrase phony numbers, but if you look at the plan and add the numbers up, these numbers are correct.

speaker: GORE
text: He spends more money for tax cuts for the wealthiest 1% than all of his new spending proposals for health care, prescription drugs, education and national defense all combined.

speaker: GORE
text: I agree that the surplus is the American people’s money, it’s your money.

speaker: GORE
text: That’s why I don’t think we should give nearly half of it to the wealthiest 1%, because the other 99% have had an awful lot to do with building the surplus in our prosperity.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Three-and-a-half minutes is up.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: New question.

text: Governor Bush, you have a question.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: This is a companion question to the question I asked Vice President Gore.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: You have questioned whether Vice President Gore has demonstrated the leadership qualities necessary to be President of the United States.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: What do you mean by that?

speaker: BUSH
text: Actually what I’ve said, Jim.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’ve said that eight years ago they campaigned on prescription drugs for seniors.

speaker: BUSH
text: And four years ago they campaigned on getting prescription drugs for seniors.

speaker: BUSH
text: And now they’re campaigning on getting prescription drugs for seniors.

speaker: BUSH
text: It seems like they can’t get it done.

speaker: BUSH
text: Now, they may blame other folks, but it’s time to get somebody in Washington who is going to work with both Republicans and Democrats to get some positive things done when it comes to our seniors.

speaker: BUSH
text: And so what I’ve said is that there’s been some missed opportunities.

speaker: BUSH
text: They’ve had a chance.

speaker: BUSH
text: They’ve had a chance to form consensus.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’ve got a plan on Medicare, for example, that’s a two-stage plan that says we’ll have immediate help for seniors and what I call immediate Helping Hand, a $48 billion program.

speaker: BUSH
text: But I also want to say to seniors, if you’re happy with Medicare the way it is, fine, you can stay in the program.

speaker: BUSH
text: But we’re going to give you additional choices like they give federal employees in the federal employee health plan.

speaker: BUSH
text: They have a variety of choices to choose, so should seniors.

speaker: BUSH
text: And my point has been, as opposed to politicizing an issue like Medicare, in other words, holding it up as an issue, hoping somebody bites it and try to clobber them over the head with it for political purposes, this year, in the year 2000, it’s time to get it done once and for all.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s what I’ve been critical about the administration for.

speaker: BUSH
text: Same with Social Security.

speaker: BUSH
text: I think there was a good opportunity to bring Republicans and Democrats together to reform the Social Security system so seniors will never go without.

speaker: BUSH
text: Those on Social Security today will have their promise made, but also to give younger workers the option at their choice of being able to manage some of their own money in the private sector to make sure there’s a Social Security system around tomorrow.

speaker: BUSH
text: There are a lot of young workers at our rallies we go to that when they hear I’ll trust them at their option to be able to manage, under certain guidelines, some of their own money to get a better rate of return so that they’ll have a retirement plan in the future, they begin to nod their heads and they want a different attitude in Washington.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: One minute rebuttal.

speaker: GORE
text: Well, Jim, under my plan all seniors will get prescription drugs under Medicare.

speaker: GORE
text: The governor has described Medicare as a government HMO.

speaker: GORE
text: It’s not, and let me explain the difference.

speaker: GORE
text: Under the Medicare prescription drug proposal I’m making, here is how it works, you go to your own doctor.

speaker: GORE
text: Your doctor chooses your prescription.

speaker: GORE
text: No HMO or insurance company can take those choices away from you.

speaker: GORE
text: Then you go to your own pharmacy.

speaker: GORE
text: You fill the prescription and Medicare pays half the cost.

speaker: GORE
text: If you’re in a very poor family or if you have very high costs, Medicare will pay all the costs, a $25 premium, and much better benefits than you can possibly find in the private sector.

speaker: GORE
text: Now here is the contrast.

speaker: GORE
text: 95% of all seniors would get no help whatsoever under my opponent’s plan for the first four or five years.

speaker: GORE
text: Now, one thing I don’t understand, Jim, is why is it that the wealthiest 1% get their tax cuts the first year, but 95% of seniors have to wait four to five years before they get a single penny?

speaker: BUSH
text: I guess my answer to that is the man is running on Medi-scare.

speaker: BUSH
text: Trying to frighten people in the voting booth.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s just not the way I think and it’s not my intentions and not my plan.

speaker: BUSH
text: I want all seniors to have prescription drugs in Medicare.

speaker: BUSH
text: We need to reform Medicare.

speaker: BUSH
text: Thereâ€™s been opportunity to do so but this administration has failed to do it.

speaker: BUSH
text: And so seniors will have not only a Medicare plan where the poor seniors will have prescription drugs paid for, but there will be a variety of options.

speaker: BUSH
text: The current system today has meant a lot for a lot of seniors, and I really appreciate the intentions of the current system as I mentioned.

speaker: BUSH
text: If you’re happy with the system you can stay in it.

speaker: BUSH
text: But there are a lot of procedures that haven’t kept up in Medicare with the current times.

speaker: BUSH
text: No prescription drug benefits, no drug therapy, no preventative medicines, no vision care.

speaker: BUSH
text: We need to have a modern system to help seniors, and the idea of supporting a federally controlled 132,000-page document bureaucracy as being a compassionate way for seniors, and the only compassionate source of care for seniors is not my vision.

speaker: BUSH
text: I believe we ought to give seniors more options.

speaker: BUSH
text: I believe we ought to make the system work better.

speaker: BUSH
text: I know this.

speaker: BUSH
text: I know it will require a different kind of leader to go to Washington to say to both Republicans and Democrats, let’s come together.

speaker: BUSH
text: You’ve had your chance, Vice President, you’ve been there for eight years and nothing has been done.

speaker: BUSH
text: My point is, is that my plan not only trusts seniors with options, my plan sets aside $3.

speaker: BUSH
text: 4 trillion for Medicare over the next ten years.

text: My plan also says it requires a new approach in Washington, D.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s going to require somebody who can work across the partisan divide.

text: If I could respond to that.

text: Under my plan I will put Medicare in an iron clad lockbox and prevent the money from being used for anything other than Medicare.

text: The governor has declined to endorse that idea even though the Republican as well as Democratic leaders in Congress have endorsed it.

text: Now here is the difference.

text: Under the governor’s plan, if you kept the same fee for service that you have now under Medicare, your premiums would go up by between 18% and 47%, and that is the study of the Congressional plan that he’s modeled his proposal on by the Medicare actuaries.

text: Let me give you one quick example.

text: There is a man here tonight named George McKinney from Milwaukee.

text: He’s 70 years old, has high blood pressure, his wife has heart trouble.

text: They have an income of $25,000 a year.

text: They can’t pay for their prescription drugs and so they’re some of the ones that go to Canada regularly in order to get their prescription drugs.

text: Under Governor Bush’s plan, they would get not one penny for four to five years and then they would be forced to go into an HMO or to an insurance company and ask them for coverage, but there would be no limit on the premiums or the deductibles or any of the terms and conditions.

speaker: BUSH
text: I cannot let this go by, the old-style Washington politics, of we’re going to scare you in the voting booth.

speaker: BUSH
text: Under my plan the man gets immediate help with prescription drugs.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s called Immediate Helping Hand.

text: Let me say something.

text: Your â€“

text: He talks about numbers.

speaker: MODERATOR

speaker: MODERATOR
text: How would you contrast your approach to preventing future oil price and supply problems like we have now to the approach of Governor Bush?

speaker: GORE
text: Excellent question.

speaker: GORE
text: And here is the simple difference.

speaker: GORE
text: My plan has not only a short-term component, but also a long-term component.

speaker: GORE
text: And it focuses not only on increasing the supply, which I think we have to do, but also on working on the consumption side.

speaker: GORE
text: Now, in the short-term we have to free ourselves from the domination of the big oil companies that have the ability to manipulate the price from OPEC when they want to raise the price.

speaker: GORE
text: And in the long-term we have to give new incentives for the development of domestic resources like deep gas in the western Gulf, like stripper wells for oil, but also renewable sources of energy.

speaker: GORE
text: And domestic sources that are cleaner and better.

text: And I’m proposing a plan that will give tax credits and tax incentives for the rapid development of new kinds of cars and trucks and buses and factories and boilers and furnaces that don’t have as much pollution, that don’t burn as much energy, and that help us get out on the cutting edge of the new technologies that will create millions of new jobs.

speaker: GORE
text: Because, when we sell these new products here, we’ll then be able to sell them overseas.

text: There is a ravenous demand for them overseas.

text: Now, another big difference is Governor Bush is proposing to open up some of our most precious environmental treasures, like the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for the big oil companies to go in and start producing oil there.

speaker: GORE
text: I think that is the wrong choice.

speaker: GORE
text: It would only give us a few months’ worth of oil and the oil wouldn’t start flowing for many years into the future.

speaker: GORE
text: I don’t think it’s a fair price to pay to destroy precious parts of America’s environment.

speaker: GORE
text: We have to bet on the future and move beyond the current technologies to have a whole new generation of more efficient, cleaner, energy technology.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s an issue I know a lot about.

text: I was a small oil person for a while in west Texas.

speaker: BUSH
text: This is an administration that’s had no plan.

text: And all of a sudden the results of having no plan have caught up with America.

text: First and foremost we have to fully fund LIHEAP which is a way to help low income folks, particularly here in the east to pay for high fuel bills.

text: Secondly, we need an active exploration program in America.

text: The only way to become less dependent on foreign sources of crude oil is to explore at home.

text: You bet I want to open up a small part of Alaska.

text: When that field is online it will produce one million barrels a day.

text: Today we import one million barrels from Saddam Hussein.

speaker: BUSH
text: I would rather that a million come from our own hemisphere, our own country as opposed to Saddam Hussein.

speaker: BUSH
text: I want to build more pipelines to move natural gas throughout this hemisphere.

speaker: BUSH
text: I want to develop the coal resources in America.

speaker: BUSH
text: Have clean coal technologies.

speaker: BUSH
text: Weâ€™ve got abundant supplies of energy here in America and weâ€™d better get after it, we better start exploring it or otherwise we’ll be in deep trouble in the future because of our dependency upon foreign sources of crude.

text: So if somebody is watching tonight and listening to what the two of you just said, is it fair to say, okay, the differences between Governor Bush and Vice President Gore are as follows.

text: You’re for doing something on the consumption end and you’re for doing something on the production end?

text: Let me clarify.

text: I’m for doing something both on the supply side and production side and on the consumption side.

text: Let me say, that I found one thing in Governor Bush’s answer that we certainly agree on, and that’s the low income heating assistance program.

text: I commend you for supporting that.

text: And to establish a permanent home heating oil reserve here in the northeast.

text: Now, as for the proposals that I’ve worked for for renewables and conservation and efficiencies and new technologies.

text: The fact is for the last few years in the Congress, we’ve faced a lot of opposition to them.

text: They’ve only approved about 10% of the agenda I’ve helped to send up there.

text: I think we need to get serious about this energy crisis, both in the Congress and in the White House, and if you entrust me with the presidency, I will tackle this problem and focus on new technologies that will make us less dependent on big oil or foreign oil.

text: How would you draw the difference?

speaker: BUSH
text: Well I would first say he should have been tackling it for the last seven years.

speaker: BUSH
text: Secondly the difference is we need to explore at home.

text: And the vice president doesn’t believe in exploration in Alaska.

text: There’s a lot of shut-in gas that we need to be moving out of Alaska by pipeline.

text: There’s an interesting issue up in the northwest as well.

text: I’m against removing dams in the northwest.

speaker: BUSH
text: I donâ€™t know where the vice president stands but thatâ€™s a renewable energy source of energy.

speaker: BUSH
text: We need to keep that in line.

speaker: BUSH
text: I was in coal country in West Virginia yesterday.

speaker: BUSH
text: There is an abundant supply of coal in America.

speaker: BUSH
text: I know we can do a better job of clean coal technologies.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’m going to ask the Congress for $2 billion to make sure we have the cleanest coal technologies in the world.

speaker: BUSH
text: My answer to you is in the short-term we need to get after it here in America.

speaker: BUSH
text: We need to explore our resources and we need to develop our reservoirs of domestic production.

speaker: BUSH
text: We also need to have a hemispheric energy policy where Canada, Mexico and the United States come together.

speaker: BUSH
text: I brought this up recently with Vincent Fox the newly elected president in Mexico, he’s a man I know from Mexico.

speaker: BUSH
text: I talked to him about how best to expedite the exploration of natural gas in Mexico and transport it up to the United States so we become less dependent on foreign sources of crude oil.

speaker: BUSH
text: This is a major problem facing America.

speaker: BUSH
text: The administration did not deal with it.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s time for a new administration to deal with the energy problem.

speaker: GORE
text: If I may just briefly, Jim, note.

speaker: GORE
text: I found a couple of other things we agree upon.

speaker: GORE
text: We may not find that many this evening, so I wanted to emphasize.

speaker: GORE
text: I strongly support new investments in clean coal technology.

speaker: GORE
text: I made a proposal three months ago on this.

speaker: GORE
text: And also domestic exploration yes, but not in the environmental treasures of our country.

speaker: GORE
text: We don’t have to do that.

speaker: GORE
text: That’s the wrong choice.

speaker: GORE
text: I know the oil companies have been itching to do that, but it is not the right thing for the future.

speaker: BUSH
text: No.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s the right thing for the consumers.

speaker: BUSH
text: Less dependency upon foreign sources of crude is good for consumers.

speaker: BUSH
text: And we can do so in an environmentally friendly way.

speaker: GORE
text: Well can I have the last word on this?

speaker: MODERATOR
text: New question, new subject.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Governor Bush.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: If elected president, would you try to overturn the FDA’s approval last week of the abortion pill RU-486?

speaker: BUSH
text: I don’t think a president can do that.

speaker: BUSH
text: I was disappointed in the ruling because I think abortions ought to be more rare in America, and I’m worried that that pill will create more abortions and cause more people to have abortions.

speaker: BUSH
text: This is a very important topic and it’s a very sensitive topic, because a lot of good people disagree on the issue.

speaker: BUSH
text: I think what the next president ought to do is to promote a culture of life in America.

speaker: BUSH
text: Life of the elderly and life of those living all across the country.

speaker: BUSH
text: Life of the unborn.

speaker: BUSH
text: As a matter of fact, I think a noble goal for this country is that every child, born or unborn, need to be protected by law and welcomed to life.

speaker: BUSH
text: I know we need to change a lot of minds before we get there in America.

speaker: BUSH
text: What I do believe is that we can find good, common ground on issues of parental consent or parental notification.

speaker: BUSH
text: I know we need to ban partial birth abortions.

speaker: BUSH
text: This is a place where my opponent and I have strong disagreement.

speaker: BUSH
text: I believe banning partial birth abortions would be a positive step to reducing the number of abortions in America.

speaker: BUSH
text: This is an issue that will require a new attitude.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’ve been battling over abortion for a long period of time.

speaker: BUSH
text: Surely this nation can come together to promote the value of life.

speaker: BUSH
text: Surely we can fight off these laws that will encourage doctors to — to allow doctors to take the lives of our seniors.

speaker: BUSH
text: Surely we can work together to create a cultural life so some of these youngsters who feel like they can take a neighbor’s life with a gun will understand that that’s not the way America is meant to be.

speaker: BUSH
text: Surely we can find common ground to reduce the number of abortions in America.

speaker: BUSH
text: As to the drug itself, I mentioned I was disappointed.

speaker: BUSH
text: I hope the FDA took its time to make sure that American women will be safe who use this drug.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Vice President Gore?

speaker: GORE
text: Well, Jim, the FDA took 12 years, and I do support that decision.

speaker: GORE
text: They determined it was medically safe for the women who use that drug.

speaker: GORE
text: This is indeed a very important issue.

speaker: GORE
text: First of all on the issue of partial birth or so-called late-term abortion, I would sign a law banning that procedure, provided that doctors have the ability to save a woman’s life or to act if her health is severely at risk.

speaker: GORE
text: That’s not the main issue.

speaker: GORE
text: The main issue is whether or not the Roe v.

speaker: GORE
text: Wade decision is going to be overturned.

speaker: GORE
text: I support a woman’s right to choose.

speaker: GORE
text: My opponent does not.

speaker: GORE
text: It is important because the next president is going to appoint three and maybe even four justices of the Supreme Court.

speaker: GORE
text: And Governor Bush has declared to the anti-choice groups that he will appoint justices in the mold of Scalia and Clarence Thomas, who are known for being the most vigorous opponents of a woman’s right to choose.

speaker: GORE
text: Here is the difference.

speaker: GORE
text: He trusts the government to order a woman to do what it thinks she ought to do.

speaker: GORE
text: I trust women to make the decisions that affect their lives, their destinies and their bodies.

speaker: GORE
text: And I think a woman’s right to choose ought to be protected and defended.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Governor, we’ll go to the Supreme Court question in a moment, but make sure I understand your position on RU-486.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: If you’re elected president, not through appointments to the FDA, you won’t support legislation to overturn this?

speaker: BUSH
text: I don’t think a president can unilaterally overturn it.

speaker: BUSH
text: The FDA has made its decision.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: That means you wouldn’t, through appointments, to the FDA and ask them to —

speaker: BUSH
text: I think once a decision has been made, it’s been made unless it’s proven to be unsafe to women.

speaker: GORE
text: Jim, the question you asked, if I heard you correctly, was would he support legislation to overturn it.

speaker: GORE
text: And if I heard the statement day before yesterday, you said you would order — he said he would order his FDA appointee to review the decision.

speaker: GORE
text: Now that sounds to me a little bit different.

speaker: GORE
text: I just think that we ought to support the decision.

speaker: BUSH
text: I said I would make sure that women would be safe who used the drug.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: On the Supreme Court question.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Should a voter assume — you’re pro-life.

speaker: BUSH
text: I am pro-life.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Should a voter assume that all judicial appointments you make to the supreme court or any other court, federal court, will also be pro-life?

speaker: BUSH
text: The voters should assume I have no litmus test on that issue or any other issue.

speaker: BUSH
text: Voters will know I’ll put competent judges on the bench.

speaker: BUSH
text: People who will strictly interpret the Constitution and not use the bench to write social policy.

speaker: BUSH
text: That is going to be a big difference between my opponent and me.

speaker: BUSH
text: I believe that the judges ought not to take the place of the legislative branch of government.

speaker: BUSH
text: That they’re appointed for life and that they ought to look at the Constitution as sacred.

speaker: BUSH
text: They shouldn’t misuse their bench.

speaker: BUSH
text: I don’t believe in liberal activist judges.

speaker: BUSH
text: I believe in strict constructionists.

speaker: BUSH
text: Those are the kind of judges I will appoint.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’ve named four supreme court justices in the State of Texas and would ask the people to check out their qualifications, their deliberations.

speaker: BUSH
text: They’re good, solid men and women who have made good, sound judgments on behalf of the people of Texas.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: What kind of appointments should they expect from you?

speaker: GORE
text: We both use similar language to reach an exactly opposite outcome.

speaker: GORE
text: I don’t favor a litmus test, but I know that there are ways to assess how a potential justice interprets the Constitution.

speaker: GORE
text: And in my view, the Constitution ought to be interpreted as a document that grows with our country and our history.

speaker: GORE
text: And I believe, for example, that there is a right of privacy in the Fourth Amendment.

speaker: GORE
text: And when the phrase a strict constructionist is used and when the names of Scalia and Thomas are used as the benchmarks for who would be appointed, those are code words, and nobody should mistake this, for saying the governor would appoint people who would overturn Roe v.

speaker: GORE
text: Wade.

speaker: GORE
text: It’s very clear to me.

speaker: GORE
text: I would appoint people that have a philosophy that I think would have it quite likely they would uphold Roe v.

speaker: GORE
text: Wade.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Is the vice president right?

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Is that a code word for overturning Roe v.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Wade?

speaker: BUSH
text: It sounds like the vice presidentâ€™s not right very many times tonight.

speaker: BUSH
text: I just told you the criteria on which I’ll appoint judges.

speaker: BUSH
text: I have a record of appointing judges in the State of Texas.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s what a governor gets to do.

speaker: BUSH
text: A governor gets to name supreme court judges.

speaker: BUSH
text: He also reads all kinds of things into my tax plan and into my Medicare plan.

speaker: BUSH
text: I want the viewers out there to listen to what I have to say about it.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Reverse the question.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: What code phrases should we read by what you said about what kind of people you would appoint?

speaker: GORE
text: It would be likely that they would uphold Roe v.

speaker: GORE
text: Wade.

speaker: GORE
text: I do believe it’s wrong to use a litmus test.

speaker: GORE
text: If you look at the history of a lower court judge’s rulings, you can get a pretty good idea of how they’ll interpret questions.

speaker: GORE
text: A lot of questions are first impression, and these questions that have been seen many times come up in a new context and so — but, you know, this is a very important issue.

speaker: GORE
text: Because a lot of young women in this country take this right for granted and it could be lost.

speaker: GORE
text: It is on the ballot in this election, make no mistake about it.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’ll tell you what kind of judges he’ll put on.

speaker: BUSH
text: He’ll put liberal activists justices who will use their bench to subvert the legislature, that’s what he’ll do.

speaker: GORE
text: Thatâ€™s not right.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: New subject, new question.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Vice President Gore, if President Milosevic of Yugoslavia refuses to accept the election results and leave office, what action, if any, should the United States take to get him out of there?

speaker: GORE
text: Well, Milosevic has lost the election.

speaker: GORE
text: His opponent, Kostunica, has won the election.

speaker: GORE
text: It’s overwhelming.

speaker: GORE
text: Milosevic’s government refuses to release the vote count.

speaker: GORE
text: There’s now a general strike going on.

speaker: GORE
text: They’re demonstrating.

speaker: GORE
text: I think we should support the people of Serbia and Yugoslavia, as they call the Serbia plus Montenegro, and put pressure in every way possible to recognize the lawful outcome of the election.

speaker: GORE
text: The people of Serbia have acted very bravely in kicking this guy out of office.

speaker: GORE
text: Now he is trying to not release the votes and then go straight to a so-called runoff election without even announcing the results of the first vote.

speaker: GORE
text: Now, we’ve made it clear, along with our allies, that when Milosevic leaves, then Serbia will be able to have a more normal relationship with the rest of the world.

speaker: GORE
text: That is a very strong incentive that we’ve given them to do the right thing.

speaker: GORE
text: Bear in mind also, Milosevic has been indicted as a war criminal and he should be held accountable for his actions.

speaker: GORE
text: Now, we have to take measured steps because the sentiment within Serbia is, for understandable reasons, against the United States because their nationalism — even if they don’t like Milosevic, they still have some feelings lingering from the NATO action there.

speaker: GORE
text: So we have to be intelligent in the way we go about it.

speaker: GORE
text: But make no mistake about it, we should do everything we can to see that the will of the Serbian people expressed in this extraordinary election is done.

speaker: GORE
text: And I hope that he’ll be out of office very shortly.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Governor Bush, one minute.

speaker: BUSH
text: Well, I’m pleased with the results of the election.

speaker: BUSH
text: As the vice president is.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s time for the man to go.

speaker: BUSH
text: It means that the United States must have a strong diplomatic hand with our friends in NATO.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s why it’s important to make sure our alliances are as strong as they possibly can be to keep the pressure on Mr.

speaker: BUSH
text: Milosevic.

speaker: BUSH
text: But this will be an interesting moment for the Russians to step up and lead as well.

speaker: BUSH
text: Be a wonderful time for the Russians to step into the Balkans and convince Mr.

speaker: BUSH
text: Milosevic that it’s in his best interest and his country’s best interest to leave office.

speaker: BUSH
text: The Russians have a lot of sway in that part of the world.

speaker: BUSH
text: We would like to see the Russians use that sway to encourage democracy to take hold.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s an encouraging election.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s time for the man to leave.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: What if he doesn’t leave?

speaker: MODERATOR
text: What if all the diplomatic efforts, all the pressure from all over the world and he still doesn’t go?

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Is this the kind of thing, to be specific, that you as president would consider the use of U.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: military force to get him gone?

speaker: GORE
text: In this particular situation, no.

speaker: GORE
text: Bear in mind that we have a lot of sanctions in force against Serbia right now.

speaker: GORE
text: And the people of Serbia know that they can escape all those sanctions if this guy is turned out of power.

speaker: GORE
text: Now, I understand what the governor has said about asking the Russians to be involved, and under some circumstances that might be a good idea.

speaker: GORE
text: But being as they have not yet been willing to recognize Kostunica as the lawful winner of the election, I’m not sure it’s right for us to invite the president of Russia to mediate this — this dispute there because we might not like the results that comes out of that.

speaker: GORE
text: They currently favor going forward with a runoff election.

speaker: GORE
text: I think that’s the wrong thing.

speaker: GORE
text: I think the governor’s instinct is not necessarily bad because we have worked with the Russians in a constructive way in Kosovo, for example, to end the conflict there.

speaker: GORE
text: But I think we need to be very careful in the present situation before we invite the Russians to play the lead role in mediating.

speaker: BUSH
text: Well obviously we wouldn’t use the Russians if they didn’t agree with our answer, Mr.

speaker: BUSH
text: Vice President.

speaker: GORE
text: They donâ€™t.

speaker: BUSH
text: Let me say this to you, I wouldn’t use force.

speaker: BUSH
text: I wouldn’t use force.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: You wouldn’t use force?

speaker: BUSH
text: No.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Why not?

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s not in our national interest to use force in this case.

speaker: BUSH
text: I would use pressure and diplomacy.

speaker: BUSH
text: There is a difference with what the president did in Kosovo which I supported and this.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s up to the people in this region to take control of their country.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: New question.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: How would you go about as president deciding when it was in the national interest to use U.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: force, generally?

speaker: BUSH
text: Well, if it’s in our vital national interests, and that means whether our territory is threatened or people could be harmed, whether or not the alliances are — our defense alliances are threatened, whether or not our friends in the Middle East are threatened.

speaker: BUSH
text: That would be a time to seriously consider the use of force.

speaker: BUSH
text: Secondly, whether or not the mission was clear.

speaker: BUSH
text: Whether or not it was a clear understanding as to what the mission would be.

speaker: BUSH
text: Thirdly, whether or not we were prepared and trained to win.

speaker: BUSH
text: Whether or not our forces were of high morale and high standing and well-equipped.

speaker: BUSH
text: And finally, whether or not there was an exit strategy.

speaker: BUSH
text: I would take the use of force very seriously.

speaker: BUSH
text: I would be guarded in my approach.

speaker: BUSH
text: I don’t think we can be all things to all people in the world.

speaker: BUSH
text: I think we’ve got to be very careful when we commit our troops.

speaker: BUSH
text: The vice president and I have a disagreement about the use of troops.

speaker: BUSH
text: He believes in nation building.

speaker: BUSH
text: I would be very careful about using our troops as nation builders.

speaker: BUSH
text: I believe the role of the military is to fight and win war and therefore prevent war from happening in the first place.

speaker: BUSH
text: So I would take my responsibility seriously.

speaker: BUSH
text: And it starts with making sure we rebuild our military power.

speaker: BUSH
text: Morale in today’s military is too low.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’re having trouble meeting recruiting goals.

speaker: BUSH
text: We met the goals this year, but in the previous years we have not met recruiting goals.

speaker: BUSH
text: Some of our troops are not well-equipped.

speaker: BUSH
text: I believe we’re overextended in too many places.

speaker: BUSH
text: And therefore I want to rebuild the military power.

speaker: BUSH
text: It starts with a billion dollar pay raise for the men and women who wear the uniform.

speaker: BUSH
text: A billion dollars more than the president recently signed into law.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s to make sure our troops are well-housed and well-equipped.

speaker: BUSH
text: Bonus plans to keep some of our high-skilled folks in the services and a commander in chief who clearly sets the mission.

speaker: BUSH
text: The mission is to fight and win war and therefore prevent war from happening in the first place.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Vice President Gore, one minute.

speaker: GORE
text: Let me tell you what Iâ€™ll do.

speaker: GORE
text: First of all Â I want to make it clear, our military is the strongest, best-trained, best-equipped, best-led fighting force in the world and in the history of the world.

speaker: GORE
text: Nobody should have any doubt about that, least of all our adversaries or potential adversaries.

speaker: GORE
text: If you entrust me with the presidency, I will do whatever is necessary in order to make sure our forces stay the strongest in the world.

speaker: GORE
text: In fact, in my ten-year budget proposal I’ve set aside more than twice as much for this purpose as Governor Bush has in his proposal.

speaker: GORE
text: Now, I think we should be reluctant to get involved in someplace in a foreign country.

speaker: GORE
text: But if our national security is at stake, if we have allies, if we’ve tried every other course, if we’re sure military action will succeed, and if the costs are proportionate to the benefits, we should get involved.

speaker: GORE
text: Now, just because we don’t want to get involved everywhere doesn’t mean we should back off anywhere it comes up.

speaker: GORE
text: I disagree with the proposal that maybe only when oil supplies are at stake that our national security is at risk.

speaker: GORE
text: I think that there are situations like in Bosnia or Kosovo where there’s a genocide, where our national security is at stake there.

speaker: BUSH
text: I agree our military is the strongest in the world today, that’s not the question.

speaker: BUSH
text: The question is will it be the strongest in the years to come?

speaker: BUSH
text: The warning signs are real.

speaker: BUSH
text: Everywhere I go on the campaign trail I see moms and dads whose son or daughter may wear the uniform and they tell me about how discouraged their son or daughter may be.

speaker: BUSH
text: A recent poll was taken among 1,000 enlisted personnel, as well as officers, over half of whom will leave the service when their time of enlistment is up.

speaker: BUSH
text: The captains are leaving the service.

speaker: BUSH
text: There is a problem.

speaker: BUSH
text: And it’s going to require a new commander in chief to rebuild the military power.

speaker: BUSH
text: The other day I was honored to be flanked by Colin Powell and General Norman Schwartzkopf recently stood by me side and agreed with me.

speaker: BUSH
text: They said even if we are the strongest if we donâ€™t do something if we don’t have a clear vision of the military, if we don’t stop extending our troops all around the world and nation building missions, then we’re going to have a serious problem coming down the road, and I’m going to prevent that.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’m going to rebuild our military power.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s one of the major priorities of my administration.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Vice President Gore, how should the voters go about deciding which one of you is better suited to make the kinds of decisions, whether it’s Milosevic or whatever, in the military and foreign policy area?

speaker: GORE
text: Well, they should look at our proposals and look at us as people and make up their own minds.

speaker: GORE
text: When I was a young man, I volunteered for the Army.

speaker: GORE
text: I served my country in Vietnam.

speaker: GORE
text: My father was a senator who strongly opposed the Vietnam War.

speaker: GORE
text: I went to college in this great city, and most of my peers felt against the war as I did.

speaker: GORE
text: But I went anyway because I knew if I didn’t, somebody else in the small town of Carthage, Tennessee, would have to go in my place.

speaker: GORE
text: I served for eight years in the House of Representatives and I served on the Intelligence Committee, specialized in looking at arms control.

speaker: GORE
text: I served for eight years in the United States Senate and served on the Armed Services Committee.

speaker: GORE
text: For the last eight years I’ve served on the National Security Council, and when the conflict came up in Bosnia, I saw a genocide in the heart of Europe with the most violent war on the continent of Europe since World War II.

speaker: GORE
text: Look, that’s where World War I started in the Balkans.

speaker: GORE
text: My uncle was a victim of poisonous gas there.

speaker: GORE
text: Millions of Americans saw the results of that conflict.

speaker: GORE
text: We have to be willing to make good, sound judgments.

speaker: GORE
text: Incidentally, I know the value of making sure our troops have the latest technology.

speaker: GORE
text: The governor has proposed skipping the next generation of weapons.

speaker: GORE
text: I think that’s a big mistake, because I think we have to stay at the cutting edge.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Governor, how would you advise the voters to make the decision on this issue?

speaker: BUSH
text: I think you’ve got to look at how one has handled responsibility in office.

speaker: BUSH
text: Whether or not it’s — the same in domestic policy as well.

speaker: BUSH
text: Whether or not you have the capacity to convince people to follow?

speaker: BUSH
text: Whether or not one makes decisions based on sound principles or whether or not you rely upon polls and focus groups on how to decide what the course of action is.

speaker: BUSH
text: We have too much polling and focus groups going on in Washington today.

speaker: BUSH
text: We need decisions made on sound principles.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’ve been the governor of a big state.

speaker: BUSH
text: I think one of the hallmarks of my relationship in Austin, Texas, is that I’ve had the capacity to work with both Republicans and Democrats.

speaker: BUSH
text: I think that’s an important part of leadership.

speaker: BUSH
text: I think what it means to build consensus.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’ve shown I know how to do so.

speaker: BUSH
text: Tonight in the audience there’s one elected state senator who is a Democrat, a former state-wide officer who is a Democrat, a lot of Democrats who are here in the debate to — because they want to show their support that shows I know how to lead.

speaker: BUSH
text: And so the fundamental answer to your question, who can lead and who’s shown the ability to get things done?

speaker: GORE
text: If I could say one thing.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: We are way over three-and-a-half minutes.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Go ahead.

speaker: GORE
text: One of the key points in foreign policy and national security policy is the need to re-establish the old-fashioned principle that politics ought to stop at the water’s edge.

speaker: GORE
text: When I was in the United States Congress, I worked with former President Reagan to modernize our strategic weaponry and to pursue arms control in a responsible way.

speaker: GORE
text: When I was in the United States Senate I worked with former President Bush, your father.

speaker: GORE
text: I was one of only a few Democrats in the Senate to support the Persian Gulf War.

speaker: GORE
text: I think bipartisanship is a national asset.

speaker: GORE
text: We have to find ways to reestablish it in foreign policy and national security policy.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Do you have a problem with that?

speaker: BUSH
text: Yeah.

speaker: BUSH
text: Why haven’t they done it in seven years?

speaker: MODERATOR
text: New subject.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: New question.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Should the voters of this election, Vice President Gore, see this in the domestic area as a major choice between competing political philosophies?

speaker: GORE
text: Oh, absolutely.

speaker: GORE
text: This is a very important moment in the history of our country.

speaker: GORE
text: Look, we’ve got the biggest surpluses in all of American history.

speaker: GORE
text: The key question that has to be answered in this election is will we use that prosperity wisely in a way that benefits all of our people and doesn’t go just to the few.

speaker: GORE
text: Almost half of all the tax cut benefits, as I said under Governor Bush’s plan, go to the wealthiest 1%.

speaker: GORE
text: I think we have to make the right and responsible choices.

speaker: GORE
text: I think we have to invest in education, protecting the environment, health care, a prescription drug benefit that goes to all seniors, not just to the poor, under Medicare, not relying on HMOs and insurance companies.

speaker: GORE
text: I think that we have to help parents and strengthen families by dealing with the kind of inappropriate entertainment material that families are just heart sick that their children are exposed to.

speaker: GORE
text: I think we’ve got to have welfare reform taken to the next stage.

speaker: GORE
text: I think that we have got to balance the budget every single year, pay down the national debt and, in fact, under my proposal the national debt will be completely eliminated by the year 2012.

speaker: GORE
text: I think we need to put Medicare and Social Security in a lockbox.

speaker: GORE
text: The governor will not put Medicare in a lockbox.

speaker: GORE
text: I don’t think it should be used as a piggy bank for other programs.

speaker: GORE
text: I think it needs to be moved out of the budget and protected.

speaker: GORE
text: I’ll veto anything that takes money out of Social Security or Medicare for anything other than Social Security or Medicare.

speaker: GORE
text: Now, the priorities are just very different.

speaker: GORE
text: I’ll give you a couple of examples.

speaker: GORE
text: For every new dollar that I propose for spending on health care, Governor Bush spends $3 for a tax cut for the wealthiest 1%.

speaker: GORE
text: Now, for every dollar that I propose to spend on education, he spends $5 on a tax cut for the wealthiest 1%.

speaker: GORE
text: Those are very clear differences.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Governor, one minute.

speaker: BUSH
text: The man is practicing fuzzy math again.

speaker: BUSH
text: There’s differences.

speaker: BUSH
text: Under Vice President Gore’s plan, he is going to grow the federal government in the largest increase since Lyndon Baines Johnson in 1965.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’re talking about a massive government, folks.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’re talking about adding to or increasing 200 programs, 20,000 new bureaucrats.

speaker: BUSH
text: Imagine how many IRS agents it is going to take to be able to figure out his targeted tax cut for the middle class that excludes 50 million Americans.

speaker: BUSH
text: There is a huge difference in this campaign.

speaker: BUSH
text: He says he’s going to give you tax cuts.

speaker: BUSH
text: 50 million of you won’t receive it.

speaker: BUSH
text: He said in his speech he wants to make sure the right people get tax relief.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s not the role of a president to decide right and wrong.

speaker: BUSH
text: Everybody who pays taxes ought to get tax relief.

speaker: BUSH
text: After my plan is in place, the wealthiest Americans will pay a higher percentage of taxes then they do today, the poorest of Americans, six million families, won’t pay any tax at all.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s a huge difference.

speaker: BUSH
text: A difference between big exploding federal government that wants to think on your behalf and a plan that meets priorities and liberates working people to be able to make decisions on your own.

speaker: GORE
text: Let me just say, Jim, you haven’t heard the governor deny these numbers.

speaker: GORE
text: He’s called them phony and fuzzy.

speaker: GORE
text: The fact remains almost 30% of his proposed tax cut goes to — only to Americans that make more than $1 million per year.

speaker: GORE
text: More money goes to the — can I have a rebuttal here?

speaker: MODERATOR
text: I want to see if he buys that.

speaker: BUSH
text: Let me tell you what the facts are.

speaker: BUSH
text: The facts are after my plan, the wealthiest of Americans pay more taxes of the percentage of the whole than they do today.

speaker: BUSH
text: Secondly, if you’re a family of four making $50,000 in Massachusetts, you get a 50% tax cut.

speaker: BUSH
text: Let me give you one example.

speaker: BUSH
text: The Strunk family in Allentown, Pennsylvania, I campaigned with them the other day.

speaker: BUSH
text: They make $51,000 combined income, they pay about $3500 in taxes.

speaker: BUSH
text: Under my plan, they get $1800 of tax relief.

speaker: BUSH
text: Under Vice President Gore’s plan, they get $145 of tax relief.

speaker: BUSH
text: Now you tell me who stands on the side of the fence.

speaker: BUSH
text: You ask the Strunks whose plan makes more sense.

speaker: BUSH
text: There is a difference of opinion.

speaker: BUSH
text: He would rather spend the family’s $1800 and I would rather the Strunks spend their own money.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Do you see it that way Mr.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Vice President?

speaker: GORE
text: No, I don’t, and I’m not going to go to calling names on his facts.

speaker: GORE
text: I’m just gonna tell you what the real facts are.

speaker: GORE
text: The analysis that he’s talking about leaves out more than half of the tax cuts that I have proposed.

speaker: GORE
text: And if you just add the numbers up, he still hasn’t denied it, he spends more money on a tax cut for the wealthiest 1% than all his new proposals for prescription drugs, healthcare, education, and national defense combined.

speaker: GORE
text: Now those are the wrong priorities.

speaker: GORE
text: $665 billion over ten years for the wealthiest 1%.

speaker: GORE
text: As I said, almost 30% of it goes to Americans that make more than $1 million per year.

speaker: GORE
text: Every middle class family is eligible for a tax cut under my proposal.

speaker: GORE
text: Let me give you some specific examples.

speaker: GORE
text: I believe college tuition up to $10,000 per year ought to be tax deductible so middle-class families can choose to send their children to college.

speaker: GORE
text: I believe all senior citizens should be able to choose their own doctors and get prescription drugs from their own pharmacists with Medicare paying half the bill.

speaker: GORE
text: I believe parents ought to be able to make more choices need more public and charter school choice to send their kids always to a safe school.

speaker: GORE
text: We need to make education the number one priority in our country and treat teachers like the professionals that they are.

speaker: GORE
text: And that’s why I have made it a number one priority in my budget, not a tax cut for the wealthy.

speaker: BUSH
text: Let me talk about tax cuts one more time.

speaker: BUSH
text: This is a man whose plan excludes 50 million Americans.

speaker: GORE
text: Not so.

speaker: BUSH
text: Take for example the marriage penalty.

speaker: BUSH
text: If you itemize your tax return, you get no marriage penalty relief.

speaker: BUSH
text: He picks and chooses.

speaker: BUSH
text: He decides who the right people are.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s a fundamental difference of opinion.

speaker: BUSH
text: I want my fellow Americans to hear one more time.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’ll spend $25 trillion — we’ll collect $25 trillion in revenue in the next 10 years and spend $21 trillion.

speaker: BUSH
text: Surely we can send 5% back to you that pay the bills.

speaker: BUSH
text: Thereâ€™s a problem wait.

speaker: BUSH
text: I want to say something, Jim.

speaker: BUSH
text: This man has been disparaging my plan with all this Washington fuzzy math.

speaker: BUSH
text: I want you to hear a problem weâ€™ve got here in the USA.

speaker: BUSH
text: If you’re a single mother making $22,000 a year and you have two children, under this tax code, for every additional dollar you make, you pay a higher marginal rate on that dollar than someone making more than $200,000 a year, and that is not right.

speaker: BUSH
text: My plan drops the rate from 15% to 10% and increases the child credit from $500 to $1,000 to make the code more fair for everybody, not just a few, not just a handful.

speaker: BUSH
text: Everybody who pays taxes ought to get some relief.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Having cleared that up, we’re going to a new question.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Education.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Governor Bush.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Both of you have promised dramatically to change — to change dramatically public education in this country.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Of the public money spent on education, only 6% of that is federal money.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: You want to change 100% of the public education with 6% of the money, is that possible?

speaker: BUSH
text: We can make a huge difference by saying if you receive federal money we expect you to show results.

speaker: BUSH
text: Let me give you a story about public education, if I might.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s about Kipp Academy in Houston, Texas.

speaker: BUSH
text: A charter school run by some people from Teach For America.

speaker: BUSH
text: Young folks saying I’m going to do something good for my country.

speaker: BUSH
text: I want to teach.

speaker: BUSH
text: A guy named Michael runs the school.

speaker: BUSH
text: It is a school full of so-called at-risk children.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s how we unfortunately label certain children.

speaker: BUSH
text: Basically it means they can’t learn.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s a school of strong discipline and high standards.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s one of the best schools in Houston.

speaker: BUSH
text: Here are the key ingredients.

speaker: BUSH
text: High expectations, strong accountabily.

speaker: BUSH
text: What Michael says, don’t put all these rules on us, just let us teach and hold us accountable for every grade.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s what we do.

speaker: BUSH
text: And as a result, these mainly Hispanic youngsters are some of the best learners in Houston, Texas.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s my vision for public education all around America.

speaker: BUSH
text: Many of you viewers don’t know, but Laura and I sent our girls to public school.

speaker: BUSH
text: They went to Austin High School.

speaker: BUSH
text: And many of the public schools are meeting the call.

speaker: BUSH
text: But, unfortunately, a lot of schools are trapping children in schools that just won’t teach and won’t change.

speaker: BUSH
text: Here is the role of the federal government.

speaker: BUSH
text: One is to change Head Start to a reading program.

speaker: BUSH
text: Two is to say if you want to access reading money, you can do so.

speaker: BUSH
text: The goal is for every single child to learn to Read.

speaker: BUSH
text: there must by K-2 diagnostic teaching tools, teacher training money, available.

speaker: BUSH
text: Three, we have to consolidate the federal programs to free districts to free the schools and encourage innovators like Michael.

speaker: BUSH
text: Let them reach out beyond the confines of the current structure to recruit teach-for-the-children type teachers.

speaker: BUSH
text: Four, we’re going to say if you receive federal money, measure third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh and eighth grade.

speaker: BUSH
text: Show us if they are learning to read, write, add and subtract and if so there will be bonus plans.

speaker: BUSH
text: But if not, instead of continuing to subsidize failure, the money will go to — the federal money will go to the parents for public school or charter school or tutorial or Catholic school.

speaker: BUSH
text: What I care about is children.

speaker: BUSH
text: And so does Michael Feinberg.

speaker: BUSH
text: And you know what?

speaker: BUSH
text: It can happen in America with the right kind of leadership.

speaker: GORE
text: We agree on a couple of things on education.

speaker: GORE
text: I strongly support new accountability, so does Governor Bush.

speaker: GORE
text: I strongly support local control, so does Governor Bush.

speaker: GORE
text: I’m in favor of testing as a way of measuring performance.

speaker: GORE
text: Every school and every school district, have every state test the children.

speaker: GORE
text: I’ve also proposed a voluntary national test in the fourth grade and eighth grade, and a form of testing the governor has not endorsed.

speaker: GORE
text: I think that all new teachers ought to be tested in the subjects that they teach.

speaker: GORE
text: We’ve got to recruit 100,000 new teachers.

speaker: GORE
text: And I have budgeted for that.

speaker: GORE
text: We’ve got to reduce the class size so that the student who walks in has more one-on-one time with the teacher.

speaker: GORE
text: We ought to have universal pre-school and we ought to make college tuition tax deductible, up to $10,000 a year.

speaker: GORE
text: I would like to tell you a quick story.

speaker: GORE
text: I got a letter today as I left Sarasota, Florida.

speaker: GORE
text: I’m here with a group of 13 people from around the country who helped me prepare.

speaker: GORE
text: We had a great time.

speaker: GORE
text: Two days ago we ate lunch at a restaurant.

speaker: GORE
text: The guy that served us lunch gave me a letter today.

speaker: GORE
text: His name is Randy Ellis.

speaker: GORE
text: He has a 15-year-old daughter named Caley, who is in Sarasota High School.

speaker: GORE
text: Her science class was supposed to be for 24 students.

speaker: GORE
text: She’s the 36th student in that classroom.

speaker: GORE
text: They sent me a picture of her in the classroom.

speaker: GORE
text: They can’t squeeze another desk in for her, so she has to stand during class.

speaker: GORE
text: I want the federal government, consistent with local control and new accountability, to make improvement of our schools the number one priority so Caley will have a desk and can sit down in a classroom where she can learn.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: All right.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: So having heard the two of you, the voters have just heard the two of you, what is the difference?

speaker: MODERATOR
text: What is the choice between the two of you on education?

speaker: BUSH
text: The first is, the difference is there is no new accountability measures in Vice President Gore’s plan.

speaker: BUSH
text: He says he’s for voluntary testing.

speaker: BUSH
text: You can’t have voluntary testing.

speaker: BUSH
text: You must have mandatory testing.

speaker: BUSH
text: You must say that if you receive money you must show us whether or not children are learning to read and write and add and subtract.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s the difference.

speaker: BUSH
text: You may claim you’ve got mandatory testing but you don’t, Mr.

speaker: BUSH
text: Vice President.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s a huge difference.

speaker: BUSH
text: Testing is the cornerstone of reform.

speaker: BUSH
text: You know how I know?

speaker: BUSH
text: Because it’s the cornerstone of reform in the State of Texas.

speaker: BUSH
text: Republicans and Democrats came together and said what can we do to make our public education the best in the country?

speaker: BUSH
text: We’ve done a long way working together to do so.

speaker: BUSH
text: The cornerstone is to have strong accountability in return for money and in return for flexibility.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’re going to ask you to show us whether or not — we ask you to post the results on the Internet.

speaker: BUSH
text: We encourage parents to take a look at the comparative results of schools.

speaker: BUSH
text: We have a strong charter school movement that I signed the legislation to get started in the State of Texas.

speaker: BUSH
text: I believe if we find poor children trapped in schools that won’t teach, we need to free the parents.

speaker: BUSH
text: We need to expand education savings accounts.

speaker: BUSH
text: Something that the vice presidentâ€™s running mate supports.

speaker: BUSH
text: There’s big differences.

speaker: BUSH
text: He won’t support freeing local districts from the strings of federal money.

speaker: GORE
text: First of all, I do have mandatory testing.

speaker: GORE
text: I think the governor may not have heard what I said clearly.

speaker: GORE
text: The voluntary national testing is in addition to the mandatory testing that we require of states.

speaker: GORE
text: All schools, all school districts, students themselves, and required teacher testing, which goes a step farther than Governor Bush has been willing to go.

speaker: GORE
text: Here are a couple of differences, though, Jim.

speaker: GORE
text: Governor Bush is in favor of vouchers which take taxpayer money away from public schools and give them to private schools that are not accountable for how the money is used and don’t have to take all applicants.

speaker: GORE
text: Now, private schools play a great role in our society.

speaker: GORE
text: All of our children have gone to both public schools and private schools.

speaker: GORE
text: But I don’t think private schools should have a right to take taxpayer money away from public schools at a time when Caley Ellis is standing in that classroom.

speaker: GORE
text: Let me give you another example.

speaker: GORE
text: I went to a school in Dade County, Florida where the facilities are so overcrowded the children have to eat lunch in shifts with the first shift for lunch starting at 9:30 in the morning.

speaker: GORE
text: Look, this is a funding crisis all around the country.

speaker: GORE
text: There are fewer parents of school-age children as a percentage of the voting population and there is the largest generation of students ever.

speaker: GORE
text: We’re in an information age when learning is more important than ever.

speaker: GORE
text: 90% of our kids go to public schools.

speaker: GORE
text: We have to make it the number one priority.

speaker: GORE
text: Modernize our schools, reduce class size, recruit new teachers, give every child a chance to learn with one-on-one time in a quality — high-quality, safe school.

speaker: GORE
text: If it’s a failing school, shut it down and reopen it under a new principal with a turnaround team of specialists the way Governor Jim Hunt does in North Carolina.

speaker: GORE
text: Here is another difference.

speaker: GORE
text: The governor, if it’s a failing school, would leave the children in that failing school for three years and then give a little bit of money to the parents, a down payment on a down payment for private school tuition, and pretend that that would be enough for them to go out and go to a private school.

speaker: GORE
text: It’s an illusion.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Wait a minute, Governor.

speaker: BUSH
text: Okay.

speaker: BUSH
text: First of all, most of good governance is at the state level.

speaker: BUSH
text: See, here is the mentality.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’m going to make the state do this and make the state do that.

speaker: BUSH
text: All I’m saying is if you spend money, show us results and test every year, which you do not do, Mr.

speaker: BUSH
text: Vice President.

speaker: BUSH
text: You don’t test every year.

speaker: BUSH
text: You can say you do to the cameras but you don’t, unless you’ve changed your plan here on the stage.

speaker: GORE
text: I didn’t say that.

speaker: BUSH
text: You need to test every year.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s how you determine if children are progressing to excellence.

speaker: BUSH
text: Secondly, one of the things that we have to be careful about in politics is throwing money at a system that has not yet been reformed.

speaker: BUSH
text: More money is needed and I spend more money, but step one is to make sure we reform the system to have the system in place that leaves no child behind.

speaker: BUSH
text: Stop this business about asking gosh, how old are you?

speaker: BUSH
text: If you’re 10 we’ll put you here, 12 you put here.

speaker: BUSH
text: Start asking the question, what do you know?

speaker: BUSH
text: If you don’t know what you’re supposed to know, we’ll make sure you do early before it’s too late.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: New question.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: We’ve been talking about a lot of specific issues.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: It’s often said that in the final analysis about 90% of being the President of the United States is dealing with the unexpected, not with issues that came up in the campaign.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Vice President Gore, can you point to a decision, an action you have taken, that illustrates your ability to handle the unexpected, the crisis under fire?

speaker: GORE
text: When the action in Kosovo was dragging on and we were searching for a solution to the problem, our country had defeated the adversary on the battlefield without a single American life being lost in combat.

speaker: GORE
text: But the dictator Milosevic was hanging on.

speaker: GORE
text: I invited the former prime minister of Russia to my house and took a risk in asking him to get personally involved, along with the head of Finland, to go to Belgrade and to take a set of proposals from the United States that would constitute basically a surrender by Serbia.

speaker: GORE
text: But it was a calculated risk that paid off.

speaker: GORE
text: Now, I could probably give you some other examples of decisions over the last 24 years.

speaker: GORE
text: I have been in public service for 24 years, Jim.

speaker: GORE
text: And throughout all that time the people I have fought for have been the middle-class families, and I have been willing to stand up to powerful interests like the big insurance companies, the drug companies, the HMOs, the oil companies.

speaker: GORE
text: They have good people and they play constructive roles sometimes, but sometimes they get too much power.

speaker: GORE
text: I cast my lot with the people even when it means that you have to stand up to some powerful interests who are trying to turn the — the policies and the laws to their advantage.

speaker: GORE
text: You can see it in this campaign.

speaker: GORE
text: The big drug companies support Governor Bush’s prescription drug proposal.

speaker: GORE
text: They oppose mine because they don’t want to get Medicare involved because they’re afraid that Medicare will negotiate lower prices for seniors who currently pay the highest prices of all.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Governor Bush?

speaker: BUSH
text: I’ve been standing up to big Hollywood, big trial lawyers.

speaker: BUSH
text: Was â€“ what was the question?

speaker: BUSH
text: It was about emergencies, wasn’t it?

speaker: MODERATOR
text: It was about — okay.

speaker: BUSH
text: You know, as governor, one of the things you have to deal with is catastrophe.

speaker: BUSH
text: I can remember the fires that swept Parker County, Texas.

speaker: BUSH
text: I remember the floods that swept our state.

speaker: BUSH
text: I remember going down to Del Rio, Texas.

speaker: BUSH
text: I have to pay the administration a compliment.

speaker: BUSH
text: James Lee Witt of FEMA has done a really good job of working with governors during times of crisis.

speaker: BUSH
text: But that’s the time when you’re tested not only — it’s the time to test your mettle, a time to test your heart when you see people whose lives have been turned upside down.

speaker: BUSH
text: It broke my heart to go to the flood scene in Del Rio where a fellow and his family got completely uprooted.

speaker: BUSH
text: The only thing I knew to do was to get aid as quickly as possible with state and federal help, and to put my arms around the man and his family and cry with them.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s what governors do.

speaker: BUSH
text: They are often on the front line of catastrophic situations.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: New question.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: There can be all kinds of crises, Governor.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: A questions for you.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: There could be a crisis, for instance, in the financial area, the stock market could take a tumble, there could be a failure of a major financial institution.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: What is your general attitude toward government intervention in such events?

speaker: BUSH
text: Well, it depends, obviously.

speaker: BUSH
text: But what I would do first and foremost, is I would get in touch with the Federal Reserve Chairman, Alan Greenspan, to find out all the facts and all the circumstances.

speaker: BUSH
text: I would have my Secretary of the Treasury be in touch with the financial centers not only here, but at home.

speaker: BUSH
text: I would make sure that key members of Congress were called in to discuss the gravity of the situation.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I would come up with a game plan to deal with it.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s what governors end up doing.

speaker: BUSH
text: We end up being problem solvers.

speaker: BUSH
text: We come up with practical, common sense solutions for problems that we’re confronted with.

speaker: BUSH
text: In this case, in the case of a financial crisis, I would gather all the facts before I made the decision as to what the government ought or ought not to do.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: Vice President Gore?

speaker: GORE
text: First I want to compliment the governor on his response to those fires and floods in Texas.

speaker: GORE
text: I accompanied James Lee Witt down to Texas when those fires broke out.

speaker: GORE
text: And FEMA has been a major flagship project of our reinventing government efforts.

speaker: GORE
text: And I agree, it works extremely well now.

speaker: GORE
text: On the international financial crises that come up, my friend, Bob Rubin, the former Secretary of Treasury is here, he’s a close advisor to me and great friend in all respects.

speaker: GORE
text: I have had a chance to work with him and Alan Greenspan and others on the crisis following the collapse of the Mexican peso.

speaker: GORE
text: When the Asian financial crisis raised the risk of world-wide recession that could affect our economy, And now, of course, the euro’s value has been dropping, but seems to be under control.

speaker: GORE
text: But it started for me in the last eight years when I had the honor of casting the tie-breaking vote to end the old economic plan here at home and put into place a new economic plan that has helped us to make some progress, 22 million new jobs, the greatest prosperity ever.

speaker: GORE
text: But it’s not good enough.

speaker: GORE
text: My attitude is you ain’t seen nothing yet.

speaker: GORE
text: We need to do more and better.

speaker: MODERATOR
text: So, Governor, would you agree there is no basic difference here on intervening — on federal government intervening in what might be seen by others to be a private financial crisis?

speaker: BUSH
text: No, there’s no difference on that.

speaker: BUSH
text: There is a difference, though, as to what the economy has meant.

speaker: BUSH
text: I think the economy has meant more for the Gore and Clinton folks than the Gore and Clinton folks have meant for the economy.

speaker: BUSH
text: I think most of the economic growth that has taken place is a result of ingenuity and hard work and entrepreneurship and that’s the role of goverment to encourage that.

speaker: BUSH
text: In terms of in response to the question, no.

speaker: GORE
text: Can I comment on that?

speaker: MODERATOR
text: You may.

speaker: GORE
